Occupational fatigue poses persistent workforce and safety risks in healthcare. Other safety–critical sectors manage fatigue through structured fatigue risk management systems (FRMS), but whether healthcare’s evidence supports similar system-level claims is unclear. This systematic review synthesized evidence on the effects, implementation, and certainty of workplace fatigue-management strategies in healthcare. PubMed, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched through 1 June 2026. Studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, synthesized narratively per Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guidance, and assessed for implementation and certainty using Proctor’s framework and GRADE. Thirty-four publications representing 32 studies were included across four strategy groups: work-schedule and duty-hour controls; multicomponent programs and education/coaching; nap and restorative-break practices; and digital monitoring and real-time countermeasures. No included study evaluated a complete, formally governed fatigue risk management system; the evidence concerned isolated or bundled workplace strategies. Naps and restorative breaks showed the most recurrent short-term signals for reduced fatigue/sleepiness and improved vigilance or cognitive performance, though findings were inconsistent; evidence for other strategies was weaker, and patient-safety, organizational, and economic outcomes were rarely evaluated. Implementation evidence concentrated on acceptability and fidelity; organizational governance, structured risk assessment, reach, cost, and sustainability were unexamined, and certainty was predominantly low or very low, with one moderate-certainty exception for increased sleep duration under reduced-duty schedules. Healthcare has thus tested individual countermeasures rather than embedded fatigue risk management within organizational practice; advancing the field requires linking local hazards to supported controls, with particular attention to the governance and risk-assessment structures that remain least developed.

Purpose - Organisations are investing substantial resources in employee well-being initiatives, yet workplace stress persists and intervention outcomes remain mixed. This review proposes an explanation by examining how digitally mediated work generates stress at the level of the work system and why individual-level regulation under-performs against it. Design/methodology/approach - The paper is an integrative review. A structured search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, PsycINFO and Google Scholar identified theoretically salient studies, which were selected purposively and analysed through thematic synthesis. The analytical corpus comprises 88 sources. Findings - Traditional workplace stressors persist, but digital infrastructure extends their reach and intensity. Digital mediation generates stress through three mechanisms: continuity (sustained exposure and restricted recovery), opacity (limited access to decision-relevant information) and asymmetry (unequal influence over data and decisions). A misalignment between system-level stress generation and individual-level stress regulation is proposed as an explanation for persistent stress despite growing investment in well-being initiatives. Originality/value - The argument is formalised in three testable propositions that specify digital configurations of demands, resources and appraisal within the Job Demands - Resources, Conservation of Resources and Transactional frameworks. Implications follow for work design, governance of algorithmic management and digital leadership development.

Generative AI is increasingly influencing how retail investors access financial information, evaluate investment alternatives, and make decisions. However, its behavioral implications remain insufficiently understood, particularly in rapidly developing digital financial markets. Against the backdrop of Saudi Arabia’s financial-sector digital transformation under Vision 2030, this study examines how Generative AI investment reliance relates to investment decision quality through perceived AI reliability, AI-Induced Investor Confidence, and AI investment overreliance. It also investigates the moderating role of Generative AI financial literacy. Drawing on Behavioral Finance Theory and Automation Bias, data collected from 497 Saudi Arabian retail investors with prior experience using Generative AI for investment-related activities were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal contrasting relationships. Generative AI investment reliance is positively associated with perceived investment decision quality, while a negative sequential indirect relationship emerges through perceived AI reliability, investor confidence, and AI overreliance. Generative AI financial literacy weakens the relationship between perceived AI reliability and investor confidence. These findings highlight a potential GenAI confidence paradox, whereby reliance on AI may support investors’ perceived decision-making quality while also being associated with behavioral vulnerabilities arising from excessive confidence and dependence. The study emphasizes the importance of critical verification, calibrated AI reliance, and financial literacy. As the evidence is drawn exclusively from Saudi Arabian retail investors, its applicability to other financial markets requires further investigation.

Zusammenfassung Der frühzeitige Berufsausstieg frühpädagogischer Fachkräfte stellt angesichts des Fachkräftemangels und eines teilweise ungedeckten Betreuungsbedarfs eine zentrale Herausforderung für die frühkindliche Bildung dar. Entscheidend für die Ableitung wirksamer Gegenmaßnahmen ist ein Verständnis der Ursachen für den Berufsausstieg. Die vorliegende Studie untersucht daher auf Basis einer quantitativen Befragung von 1566 ehemaligen frühpädagogischen Fachkräften in Österreich die Gründe für ihren Berufsausstieg sowie deren Zusammenhänge mit der subjektiv eingeschätzten Rückkehrwahrscheinlichkeit in das Berufsfeld. Es ließen sich acht zentrale Dimensionen der Ausstiegsgründe identifizieren: unzureichende strukturelle Rahmenbedingungen, Personalmangel, gesellschaftliche Rahmenbedingungen, fehlende Weiterbildungsmöglichkeiten, Aspekte der Organisationsqualität, Probleme in der Zusammenarbeit im Team und mit dem Träger, gesundheitliche Belastungen sowie persönliche Gründe. Dabei zeigte sich ein kumulatives Zusammenspiel verschiedener Faktoren: Fachkräfte, die strukturelle Gründe angaben, nannten häufiger auch gesundheitliche Gründe für ihren Ausstieg. Gesundheitliche Belastungen sowie fehlende Weiterbildungsmöglichkeiten waren zudem signifikant mit einer niedrigeren Rückkehrwahrscheinlichkeit assoziiert. Diese Befunde erweitern den bisherigen Forschungsstand um eine quantitative Perspektive auf tatsächlich erfolgte Berufsausstiege und verdeutlichen, dass insbesondere strukturelle Verbesserungen, attraktive Weiterbildungsangebote sowie gezielte Maßnahmen der Gesundheitsförderung zentral sind, um frühpädagogische Fachkräfte im Beruf zu halten bzw. zurückzugewinnen.

Purpose: Archival professionals in archival institutions, records managers at organizations that create archival material, and employees of archival service providers face numerous professional challenges and the associated decision-making processes. This raises the question of whether they possess the professional and operational competence to make responsible decisions and provide expert advice on comprehensive records management within rapidly evolving physical, hybrid, or electronic environments. The primary aim of this paper is to determine the essential profiles and skill sets required for archival professionals. It addresses how to acquire and enhance professional archival expertise and what type of educational system should be pursued to ensure that the results of archival work are ethically sound, as well as sustainable and useful in the long term.Method / approach: The paper presents a conceptual and interdisciplinary analysis based on a narrative examination of archival literature, relevant regulations, and selected sources from organizational and educational psychology, supplemented by professional experience in archival education and training. These sources inform a proposed modular lifelong education framework, which is examined through an author-developed qualitative SWOT analysis. The psychological component identifies proposed conditions supporting motivation, participation in learning, and the transfer of learning to practice. The framework has not been empirically tested.Results: A conceptual framework for lifelong education is proposed for professionals working in archival institutions, records-creating organizations, and archival service providers. The framework connects degree programmes, shorter assessed learning opportunities leading to micro-credentials, and complementary non-formal learning. It aims to support professional specialization and the updating of knowledge across the records lifecycle. The psychological analysis identifies motivation, supportive learning relationships, and workplace conditions for applying acquired knowledge as important considerations in programme design. These are proposed features and implementation conditions, rather than demonstrated outcomes of an evaluated educational intervention.Conclusions / findings: This paper presents a framework for the modular education of archival professionals at both operational and university levels. It is grounded in a study of archival subjects across all three academic cycles, complemented by a system of micro-credentials and various forms of non-formal education. This approach could support a flexible and efficient education system for archival professionals and records managers, with clearly defined quality assurance and recognition procedures and the capacity to adapt to the profession’s evolving needs. Simultaneously, it would ensure transparency regarding the specific professional competencies required in particular environments and the associated labor market. All of this would be achieved while upholding the highest standards of formal education and providing access to state-of-the-art resources for acquiring the knowledge and skills essential to modern archival theory and practice.

Objective To quantify the correspondence between pilots’ post-task workload and situation-awareness ratings and instructor competency ratings during real flight. Background Adaptive systems, neuroergonomic classifiers, and competency-based training all need cognitive-state labels. Self-reports capture felt demand and awareness; instructor evaluations capture behaviorally inferred competence. Method Forty pilots completed five Cessna 172 tasks during dedicated research flights. After each task, pilots gave single-item 0–10 ratings of workload and situation awareness. One flight instructor at each of the two participating organizations rated Situation Awareness and Workload Management on 1–4 International Civil Aviation Organization-aligned scales, and rated task execution with behavior-specific items, before hearing the self-ratings. Analyses used Spearman correlations with participant-clustered bootstrap intervals, within-person decomposition, and mixed-model and stratified sensitivity analyses. Results Pooled cross-source correspondence was weak for situation awareness ( ρ = . 08 ) and workload ( ρ = − . 14 ; . 14 aligned). The two instructor competencies were strongly intercorrelated ( ρ = . 61 ) and strongly associated with same-instructor task-execution ratings ( ρ = . 69 and . 72 ). A small within-person workload signal ( r = − . 19 ) attenuated after double centering. Point estimates were similar in both strata and after excluding pilots aged 60 or older. Conclusion The two sources provided distinct, non-substitutable labels. Their strong link to same-rater task-execution scores is consistent with execution-referenced judgment, though shared-rater variance cannot be ruled out; self-reports captured pilots’ reported experience. Application Cognitive-state monitoring and training assessment should use multi-source labels and should not treat observation-based competency ratings as direct measures of internal workload or situation awareness.

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyze the relationship between students' personal and social competencies with teachers' teaching styles and to measure the contribution of both competencies in predicting variations in teaching styles. The study used a quantitative approach with a correlational design involving 57 respondents. Data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire that included indicators of personal competency, social competency, and teachers' teaching styles. Data analysis was conducted using multiple linear regression to identify the strength of the relationship and the contribution of the two predictor variables. The results showed a multiple correlation coefficient (R) of 0.976, a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.952, and an Adjusted R Square of 0.950. The simultaneous test produced an F value of 531.675 with a significance level of p less than 0.001. These findings indicate that students' personal and social competencies simultaneously have a very strong and significant predictive relationship with teachers' teaching styles, and are able to explain 95.2% of the variation. This study concludes that students' personal and social characteristics need to be considered in developing adaptive, participatory, and responsive learning practices to students' needs.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into digital news presentation, understanding how audiences interpret AI-related production cues is critical to explaining evaluations of journalistic authority and reliance. Yet existing research has largely focused on transparency and generalized trust, leaving the relationships among production cues, perceived journalistic attributes, cognitive authority, and context-dependent reliance insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we propose a Signal–Attribute–Authority–Conditional Reliance (SAAC) framework and evaluate it across three complementary studies involving Chinese digital-news users: a 2 × 2 randomized experiment manipulating AI-disclosure and human editorial-review cues while holding the underlying AI-produced news stimulus constant ( n = 473); a cross-sectional survey integrating structural modeling, predictive analysis, and necessary condition analysis ( n = 522); and explanatory semi-structured interviews ( n = 29). The experiment showed that production cues influenced several post-exposure evaluations despite identical news content. Survey findings revealed associations linking perceived disclosure quality and human editorial oversight to perceived news quality and accountability, with further associations involving journalistic cognitive authority, conditional reliance, and acceptance intention, although explanatory and predictive performance remained modest. Interviews indicated that participants distinguished technological presentation capability from journalistic source qualification and evaluated reliance in relation to news topics, perceived stakes, editorial involvement, and institutional safeguards. Together, the findings suggest that,within the present study settings, AI-mediated news acceptance is better understood as an I nstitutionally situated and conditionally bounded judgment than as a simple function of transparency or generalized trust.

documents.abstract: AI assistants in sales conversations predict conversion probabilities at each turn, but miscalibrated confidence can undermine human–AI handoff decisions. We propose Progressive Trajectory-Aware Calibration (PTAC), a lightweight post-hoc method that adjusts temperature using conversation progress and observed probability trajectories. PTAC requires fewer than 5,000 parameters. On e-commerce data with independently verified outcomes, PTAC reduced turn-stratified calibration error by over 80% at 14% purchase prevalence and by 9% relative to static scaling at the natural 6% prevalence, matching adaptive scaling. It reduced error by 63–78% on call-center data with model-generated labels and by 13% on synthetic dialogues. PTAC improved handoff error rates at fixed human workloads and reduced misplaced reliance at operational thresholds; trust outcomes were simulated and matched-trust performance was comparable. Causal-progress ablation supported deployment-time improvements on call-center and synthetic data; e-commerce gains depended on non-causal turn position.

Background : Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce fluent, context-responsive explanations and clinical suggestions, but the same fluency can conceal factual, evidentiary, or reasoning errors. Health professions students therefore need more than access skills or generic warnings: they need repeated practice deciding when AI advice is warranted, when it requires verification, and when it should be rejected. Aim : To propose a theory-informed, operational framework for teaching appropriate reliance on GenAI through case-based learning. Approach : A focused critical synthesis integrated four bodies of scholarship: GenAI in health professions education, trust and automation bias in human-AI interaction, metacognition and self-regulated learning, and case-based learning. The purpose was conceptual integration rather than exhaustive evidence retrieval or estimation of intervention effects. Framework : Verification-Scaffolded Case-Based Learning (VS-CBL) is a six-phase cycle: Commit, Consult, Challenge, Corroborate, Calibrate, and Consolidate. Students first make and rate an unaided judgment, then consult a documented AI system. They actively test the response for omissions and counterevidence, verify pivotal claims against authoritative sources, decide whether to accept, modify, or reject the advice, and complete an accountable final response plus an unaided transfer task. Faculty prevalidate cases, vary AI accuracy and error subtlety, preserve patient privacy, and scale oversight to clinical risk. Implications : VS-CBL shifts the educational target from AI use or satisfaction to appropriate reliance. It supports measurement of overreliance, underreliance, verification quality, confidence-accuracy calibration, reasoning quality, and delayed independent transfer. The design is adaptable across medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, rehabilitation, public health, and allied health programmes, including settings with limited connectivity. Conclusion : The educational question is not whether students should trust GenAI in general, but whether trust is warranted for a particular claim, task, and level of risk. VS-CBL offers a testable curriculum architecture for making that judgment visible and teachable. Its effectiveness and implementation burden require prospective, multicentre evaluation.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce polished mathematical solutions, executable code, persuasive media, and professional recommendations, yet fluency does not establish correctness, provenance, security, or contextual fitness. Existing AI-literacy frameworks appropriately describe broad competencies, while emerging studies in mathematics, programming, and health professions education show the value of domain-specific validation. What remains underdeveloped is a portable instructional process that makes verification, uncertainty, and reliance observable across disciplines. This conceptual article introduces TRACE-AI: Translate the task and stakes; Represent the problem, assumptions, and constraints; Audit the AI's reasoning and output; Corroborate pivotal claims through independent evidence, tests, or tools; Estimate uncertainty and warranted reliance; Act proportionately by accepting, revising, rejecting, or escalating; and Internalize learning through reflection and unaided transfer. The framework was developed through a theory-informed critical synthesis of AI literacy, mathematical problem solving, computational thinking and debugging, epistemic cognition, self-regulated learning, and trust calibration. Each stage produces an assessable artefact, and a risk gate increases verification and human oversight as uncertainty, irreversibility, or potential harm rises. Worked applications in mathematics, programming/cybersecurity, and health-professional reasoning demonstrate invariant functions with discipline-specific standards of proof. An assessment architecture distinguishes final-answer quality from process quality, appropriate reliance, confidence calibration, verification quality, and delayed unaided transfer. Six propositions define a research programme for comparative and randomized evaluation. TRACE-AI is not presented as an effectiveness-tested intervention; it is a transdisciplinary curriculum and research architecture requiring contextual adaptation and empirical validation. Its contribution is to move GenAI education beyond prompt production toward disciplined human judgment about when AI output deserves trust.

documents.abstract: Generation Z is increasingly a significant contributor to the Malaysian workforce and there is an urgency for organisations to understand the factors that contribute to young people being satisfied in their work. This concept paper is an integrated framework of Work Environment (WE), Autonomous Work Motivation (AWM), and Job Satisfaction (JS) for Generation Z employees in Malaysia. The model is based on the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory and the Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Work environment is conceptualised as a multidimensional set of physical, social, and organisational conditions that provide employees with job resources, while autonomous work motivation refers to engaging in work because it is intrinsically interesting or personally valued. The framework contains three relationships: Job satisfaction is positively related to a supportive work environment, autonomous work motivation is positively related to job satisfaction, and a supportive work environment is positively related to autonomous work motivation. The third relationship serves as a foundation for further testing of autonomous motivation as a mediator between work environment and job satisfaction. The importance of studying flexibility, development, autonomy, supportive relations and meaningful work as a whole, rather than separately, is warranted by recent evidence on the values of the generation Z and on employment conditions in Malaysia. The paper makes a contribution by combining two complementary theoretical lenses in a Malaysian context for Generation Z and by proposing a testable mechanism by which workplace resources might help to increase job satisfaction.

The research on the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and labour markets has focused on a limited range of areas, including the exposure of jobs to automation, the displacement of jobs, reskilling and the response of firms and public policy, leaving the question of why some labour markets are more resilient to disruption caused by AI than others largely unclear. The paper provides a thematic narrative review of peer-reviewed studies and institutional reports, which were selected purposively, and which bear directly on the links between AI, work and labour market outcomes, and which were published, primarily, between 2015 and 2026 and analysed using combined inductive/deductive thematic coding. Themes that appear in the context of each six are: AI automation intensity, human adaptability capacity, continuous reskilling ecosystems, organisational transition support, policy and institutional preparedness, and human-AI collaboration readiness. These themes are combined with the result of the analysis of labour market resilience and the HARMONY framework (Human Adaptability and Reskilling Mechanisms for Occupational Navigation in Yielding AI Economies) is developed, along with six propositions to be tested empirically, which includes a proposed mediating role of human-AI collaboration readiness. The paper brings together previously disjointed research streams in a relational fashion, provides an explicit description of the selection and coding of the sources, and puts forward a research agenda, including a proposed measurement instrument. It provides policy implications for policy makers, employers and education providers.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded within learning tasks, yet interaction frequency reveals little about cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue. Little is known about how such engagement is situated within task workflows or how dialogue characteristics and subsequent task activity relate to students' behaviour and task outcomes. This study examined cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue, its position within task workflows, and associations of dialogue and task-process characteristics with post-dialogue activity and task outcomes. Data were collected from 1,681 students across 40 university courses using three AI companions embedded in resource creation, peer moderation, and practice. Cognitive engagement in 829 conversation threads was coded with a dialogue-oriented Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, and 2,969 task sequences were modelled with first-order Markov models. Regression models linked dialogue and task-process characteristics to behavioural re-engagement, peer-rated artefact quality, and practice performance. Passive and Active engagement predominated, although resource creation involved more Constructive and Interactive dialogue, peer moderation more Passive, and practice more Active, while higher-engagement dialogue was less often followed by session termination. In resource creation, student-composed messages were associated with more dialogue-to-task returns than template-only requests at the same Passive level, whereas deeper cognitive engagement was associated with higher final artefact quality independent of return frequency; in practice, AI dialogue after an incorrect attempt was associated with fewer further attempts but higher next-attempt correctness among continuers. Post-dialogue activity and task outcomes are distinct aspects of AI use that interaction frequency cannot capture and evaluations should assess separately.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption can improve banking operations while unsettling employees’ roles, professional identities, and sense of value. This qualitative multiple-case study examined adoption strategies that bank executives may employ to enhance employees’ jobs and self-worth in commercial banks. Sociotechnical systems theory and stakeholder theory guided semi-structured interviews with professionals from seven banks. Each participant constituted a case. Interview data were supplemented by document reviews and reflexive field notes and analyzed through hybrid deductive–inductive coding, within-case pattern matching, and cross-case synthesis. Six themes emerged: system effectiveness through structured design; integration stress and job insecurity; limited stakeholder participation and transparency; varied engagement and capability building; balancing profitability and Human-in-the-Loop values; and external pressures and emergent context. Participants described operational benefits alongside uneven training, restricted employee voice, and uncertainty about career continuity. More supportive accounts emphasized human oversight, leadership communication, learning opportunities, and redeployment. The findings informed of a proposed Human-in-the-Loop AI Integration Wheel connecting inclusive strategy, sociotechnical design, workforce integration, and Human-in-the-Loop evaluation within an adaptive contextual hub. The framework offers a basis for executive planning and future testing; the study did not establish causal effects or validate the framework’s effectiveness.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes consequential decisions, yet predictive accuracy is not a sufficient justification for delegated authority. This conceptual study develops an integrated framework for assessing just AI across normative, data, model, and governance layers. Drawing on plural theories of justice, sociotechnical fairness research, and publicly available governance standards, it maps six justice requirements to observable evidence, decision rights, and remedies. It proposes a two-stage evaluation rule: exclude uses that fail independently justified minimum rights constraints, then compare eligible alternatives across multiple performance and governance criteria. As an explicitly limited normative analogy, Genesis chapter 2 motivates a Forbidden-Boundary Principle (FBP), under which an AI agent must not execute externally consequential actions outside pre-authorized boundaries. The resulting First-Principle Safe-Stop Protocol (FPSSP) comprises an independently governed policy monitor, a mandatory execution gate, a restricted or alternative safe-state controller, immutable-oriented audit trails, and accountable human authorization for recovery. We distinguish this normative and traceability contribution from existing Simplex and runtime assurance architectures; we do not claim a novel safety switch or formal proof of universal ethical compliance. A policy schema, threat model, test matrix, outcome definitions, and a prospective comparison design make the proposal falsifiable. No FPSSP implementation, experimental dataset, numerical improvement, or verified latency bound is reported. The framework supports future evaluation rather than constituting evidence of operational safety.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.

Situation awareness is fundamental to effective decision making in dynamic, uncertain, and information‐rich environments. While Endsley's three‐level situation awareness model introduced in 1995 defines the functions of perception, comprehension, and projection, the recurring information behaviors through which awareness is developed, maintained, and revised remain comparatively underspecified. This paper develops a conceptual framework integrating situation awareness and information behavior theories. The framework identifies and links triggers, information behaviors, evaluative judgments, and outcomes through four recurring mechanisms that explain how actors recognize information deficiencies, engage with and evaluate information, revise understanding, and determine whether understanding is sufficient for action. The framework extends existing situation awareness models by providing greater behavioral specificity while retaining Endsley's recursive conception of situation awareness. Six theoretical propositions are derived from the framework to guide future empirical research, and the framework identifies implications for communication and information systems. Collectively, the paper provides a more behaviorally grounded explanation of how situation awareness is maintained and revised in complex socio‐technical environments.

Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation. People often autonomously organize their own learning into "blocks": they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on. Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice. In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions. We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering professional practice and adult learning rapidly, yet its effect on the creative and intellectual potential of young specialists is contested: AI can personalise learning and stimulate idea generation, but uncritical reliance may encourage cognitive offloading and weaken independent reasoning. This study examines how AI systems can strengthen, rather than replace, the independent thinking of young professionals, taking in-service training in Uzbekistan’s mining and geology sector as a case. A qualitative, document-based design combined national regulations, international guidance, peer-reviewed literature from a structured search of Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (2019–2026), and institutional records; 35 sources were analysed. Five educational functions of AI were identified: personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, simulation, generative assistance, and data analysis. A matrix links each function to its contribution, principal risk, and pedagogical safeguard, and four principles of “human-controlled AI” are proposed: transparency, verifiability, accountability, and developmental use. Mapping a sectoral AI course against the matrix showed an emphasis on generative content creation, with data analysis and tutoring underdeveloped; a three-module structure covering AI literacy, creative work with generative tools, and geological data analysis is therefore proposed. The findings are conceptual and require empirical validation with trainee-level measures.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in work, there is a need to understand employees’ beliefs about whether it can be relied upon in occupational settings. This study developed an eight-item Workplace AI Trust Scale and examined its preliminary measurement properties and associations with workplace AI experience. Polish working adults completed an online questionnaire, and separate randomly selected subsamples were used for exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. The findings supported a common factor underlying the trust items and their empirical distinction from a supplementary distrust block. Internal consistency was high, although model fit was not uniformly favorable across all analyses. Changes in scaled fit indices provided qualified support for equal thresholds and loadings across exposure groups, although concerns about configural fit remained. Direct AI use was positively associated with trust, whereas the association with usage frequency was less consistent across analytical specifications. The reported presence of an organizational AI policy showed no statistically significant association with trust. Including the trust score improved average classification performance for AI-use frequency, but overall predictive performance remained limited. The findings support further investigation of the scale as a research instrument, while leaving its external convergent validity, broader discriminant validity, and suitability for group comparisons to be established.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.

Longitudinal evidence about the psychological impact of conversational AI use remains scarce. We report a survey study of 114 adults who reported their level of problematic AI use one year after reporting their motivations (for escape, social, entertainment, and instrumental reasons) for engaging with AI. We found high levels of AI motivation of all types predicted later problematic AI use, especially when participants turned to AI for managing their feelings and overcoming difficulties. Our findings imply that AI motivation could be used as an early warning signal of potential problematic use, especially if individuals engage with AI for emotional purposes over time.

The swift adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has transformed student learning, presenting unparalleled opportunities for automated drafting, syntactic polish, and literature synthesis, while introducing profound vulnerabilities regarding algorithmic hallucinations, cognitive offloading, and threats to academic integrity. This conceptual paper addresses critical gaps in technology acceptance literature by proposing an integrative model that positions AI literacy as a pivotal cognitive and evaluative mediating mechanism between multidimensional AI usage and academic productivity. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), and contemporary AI literacy frameworks, the paper decouples raw technological interaction from substantive educational attainment. We demonstrate that while system usage directly enhances operational task completion velocity, substantive scholarly productivity—defined by analytical depth, critical rigor, and epistemic accuracy—depends upon multidimensional AI literacy (technical understanding, effective prompting, critical output evaluation, and ethical reflexivity). Four refined theoretical propositions are formulated, accounting for competing explanatory mediators (such as academic motivation, prior academic achievement, and institutional support) and contextual moderating boundaries (academic discipline, year of study, and premium tool access). To bridge conceptual theory and empirical practice, operational definitions and a comprehensive measurement item pool are provided alongside an illustrative dual-scenario analysis. Finally, specific contextual considerations for Malaysian higher education, an expanded discussion of germane load reduction hazards, a structured limitations section, and a rigorous time-lagged PLS-SEM empirical validation blueprint are detailed for future researchers, educators, and university administrators

PURPOSE: Incorporating task-level autonomy into teleoperation systems for robot assisted laparoscopic surgery requires operators to effectively manage transitions from task-level autonomy to teleoperation control, particularly during system failures. This study investigated the impact of the level of guidance during take-over situations on participants' performance and their trust in the teleoperation system. METHODS: N = 34 students, unfamiliar with the system and task, performed a ring transfer task under two conditions: visual guidance, where they monitored the system visually, and visuo-haptic guidance, where they also received haptic feedback by holding the input device as the system operated in task-level autonomy. During some trials, system failures occurred, requiring participants to take over control. RESULTS: Results showed that participants noticed system failures faster with visuo-haptic guidance compared to visual guidance. Although visuo-haptic guidance did not improve task completion times or accuracy during task completion, it led to significantly higher trust in the teleoperation system and a stronger sense of perceived control. However, participants also reported higher physical demand and effort under visuo-haptic guidance, indicating an increased workload in this condition. CONCLUSION: In conclusion, these findings reveal important trade-offs of the influence of haptic guidance during human oversight of teleoperated autonomous systems.

Neurofeedback delivered through virtual and mixed reality has moved out of the clinic into sport, classroom, workplace-training, and consumer-wellness settings, but these four streams of literatures grow in near-isolation and cite one another rarely. We set out to read them against one technical grid, and report both what the grid shows and where the published reports do not fill it in. Reporting follows the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews, with PRISMA 2020 flow accounting. A Scopus search run on 12 May 2026 returned 131 records; 116 unique records were screened, 66 full texts were assessed, and 34 studies were retained, 32 from the database arm and two recovered by backward citation chasing. An independent second reviewer re-applied the eligibility criteria to the full text of every retained study. Eligibility was confirmed for 27 studies, which form the main analysis set, and could not be confirmed for seven, which are reported separately and enter only the sensitivity analyses. Consumer wellness supplies 18 of the 27 studies, education seven, and sport and professional training one each. Two reports are conceptual or architectural and are held out of every quantitative summary, leaving 25 empirical reports. Of those 25, the targeted outcome is stated in all 25 and the delivery medium in 21, but only 15 describe the EEG-to-environment coupling clearly enough to be classified as closed-loop, and only eight name the EEG feature used as the online control variable. Both counts are lower bounds on the corresponding properties of the systems, not point estimates. None of the seven records of unconfirmed eligibility discloses either field, so including them leaves both counts, and the conclusions drawn from them, as they are. No report could be classified as open-loop on affirmative evidence. A sensitivity search screened in duplicate, which dropped the machine-learning negation, the year bound, and the domain vocabulary (372 records; Cohen’s κ=0.66 at title and abstract), yielded 18 further eligible studies, and a uniform re-assessment of the contextual studies added 2 more. The search extends coverage and tests the robustness of the findings to the search strategy; it cannot be used to validate the full-text exclusions of the original search, because the identities of the excluded reports were not retained. In that set, 14 of 17 empirical reports name the control feature, which locates the reporting deficit in the application-oriented literature rather than in EEG-driven immersive feedback as a whole. Four of the eight disclosed control variables in the main corpus are alpha-band measures, and none of the eight comes from sport or education. The question most often asked of this literature, namely how many of these systems genuinely close the loop, therefore cannot be answered from the application-oriented record as it stands. We set out a five-field minimum reporting set that would make it answerable, and we propose, as a hypothesis for future testing rather than as a finding of this review, that the scarcity of EEG markers surviving promotion from offline correlate to online control variable is the constraint that organizes the field. The key charted fields of all 34 retained studies were re-assessed by the independent second reviewer; agreement was fair for loop topology (κ=0.40) and at chance for whether the control feature is named, because the second reviewer consistently read the reports more permissively than the written rules allow.

Digital nudging increasingly shapes behavior, impressions, and decision-making in public spaces. However, existing empirical research has largely focused on nudging in relation to individualized decision-making, offering limited insight into how diverse publics interpret such technologies when embedded in public infrastructures—what we refer to here as infrastructural digital nudging. In such settings, the influence of digital nudging may become less visible and less easily avoidable, while asymmetries between those who design the technology and those who encounter it may become more consequential. These conditions, together with the possibility that public expectations and social implications extend beyond expert-defined frameworks, highlight the need for early engagement. In this study, we investigate public perceptions of infrastructural digital nudging based on multi-display signage through a demonstration conducted at a national science museum in Japan. We used a convergent mixed-methods design that combined quantitative analyses of structured questionnaire responses with qualitative analyses of open-ended questionnaire responses and sticky notes. This research design enabled both statistical analysis and fine-grained interpretation of participants’ concerns, interests, and imagined uses. Our results show that, at an aggregate level, participants prioritized understanding the technology’s mechanisms, purposes, and social impacts over canonical ethical categories such as autonomy and transparency. However, qualitative analyses revealed considerable heterogeneity: some participants expressed strong concerns about unconscious influence, manipulation, and misuse. Co-occurrence analyses further indicated that participants’ evaluations were structured around different perspectives, including science-focused assessment and social concerns. These findings suggest that public perceptions of infrastructural digital nudging are heterogeneous and organized around multiple perspectives, not reducible to expert-defined categories. This underscores the importance of empirically examining how such technologies are interpreted when encountered in environments approximating real-world situations.

documents.abstract: Big techs and researchers increasingly claim that their training datasets are too large to inspect for bias and ethical problems. However, in the race to build ever-large models, they have relied on automated web scraping and no human curation. Datasets built this way absorb the stereotypes, exclusionary norms, and historical prejudices of their sources, and the models trained on them can reproduce and amplify those patterns. Because manually auditing billions of samples is humanly impossible, we need practical, effective methods to identify biases in these datasets. This paper studies the feasibility of ethically auditing large datasets through small samples and proposes a practical method for identifying structural biases by applying AI Ethics Tools (AIETs) to random samples. We applied Datasheets for Datasets, Data Statements, Data Nutrition Labels, and Data Cards to a 1% sample of Framed Multi30K, and Datasheets for Datasets to two 0.00006% samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe. Our results show that evaluating small samples with AIETs can reveal ethical problems, structural biases, and technical inconsistencies. Although industry practice assumes that identifying problems requires analyzing the entire dataset, we show that a random subset supports a viable qualitative analysis without overwhelming computational or human resources. Demonstrating that a dataset is biased does not require examining every instance: if a bias appears in a random sample, it is a flaw of the creation process. The AIETs' questions acted as provocateurs, evoking different perspectives and analysis methods for the same dataset, but the analysis and its results depended fundamentally on the human factor. We hope these findings contribute to urgent public discussions about ethics, transparency, accountability, and AI regulation by offering a practical pathway for responsibly auditing massive datasets.

documents.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is an increasingly common tool for investigating human responses to emergency situations. Nonetheless, studies validating and comparing human subject behavior during real world emergencies to their responses in VR are notably rare, and no prior studies have validated whether human emergency responses to guidance from a robot are comparable in VR versus the real world. In the present pre-registered study, we used VR to replicate a previous robot-guided emergency evacuation study conducted in the real world and compared human subject behavior in matched physical and virtual environments. In both environments, human subjects were asked to follow a robot to a location and to then read an article. While reading, a fire alarm sounds. The robot then attempted to guide them to a distant, unfamiliar exit rather than a nearby and familiar exit. We observed close correspondences between evacuee exit choice (the robot’s distant exit versus closer exits), evacuation time, and self-reported trust in the robot between the VR and physical environments. We further demonstrate that data collected in virtual reality can be used to create accurate motion models (mean positional error of 0.42 meters) predicting evacuee trajectories and locations in the physical environment.

documents.abstract: Social media can offer benefits for people with dementia, including enhanced social connectivity, peer support, and access to information. However, digital exclusion remains an issue, and little is known about factors that deter engagement. This study explored barriers to social media use from the perspectives of people with dementia and their unpaid carers. An online survey was completed by 227 participants (179 carers; 48 people with dementia), including questions about attitudes toward social media. Reflexive thematic analysis of open responses generated six themes: (1) Perceived value of social media; (2) Generational and age-limiting beliefs; (3) Digital access and literacy; (4) Perceived (un)safety of social media; (5) Symptoms of dementia; (6) Heavy caring loads. Social, cognitive, and technological factors perpetuate exclusion from social media among people with dementia. Addressing these barriers requires improved digital access, literacy, and safety, alongside more inclusive platform design and support for carers facilitating engagement.

The strategic shift toward community-based healthcare, away from hospital settings, is a policy priority internationally. Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) may support this transition, yet its practical applications remain underexplored. This scoping review maps CAI capabilities and their configuration within community care. We searched PubMed, the ACM Digital Library, and selected grey-literature sources for studies published from January 2023 to June 2025. Of 551 records identified, 29 studies were included. We identified 20 capabilities across five functional domains: Understand (n = 5), Transform (n = 3), Remember (n = 3), Generate (n = 5), and Act (n = 4). Findings suggest that CAI extends rather than replaces human care, supporting access, ongoing engagement, and care coordination. Multi-party and expert-in-the-loop designs emerged as recurring implementation strategies. They also surface design tensions, including tradeoffs between reliability and conversational flexibility, and between the benefits of long-term memory and associated privacy risks. The resulting capability-centered taxonomy offers accessible framework for integrating CAI into community care settings.

documents.abstract: Efficiently adapting voice control functions in smart vehicles remains a practical challenge in human-computer interaction. This study established a three-source, lightweight research system comprising user questionnaire survey (N = 326), engineer evaluation from the corporate sector (N = 12), and expert interviews from the industry (N = 8). A six-dimensional weighted adaptability assessment model(SWAAM) was designed (safety risk 30%, operational complexity 20%, usage frequency 15%, command clarity 15%, feedback requirements 10%, and technical feasibility 10%). Within 15 days, a systematic evaluation of 30 vehicle control functions was completed. The results indicate that user voice preference exhibits significant stratification: preference rates for high-frequency comfort functions such as navigation, air conditioning, and media exceed 98%, while preference rates for safety-critical functions such as driver assistance and chassis control are below 60%. Through triangulation validation, 15 items were identified for the whitelist (priority for release), 3 for the blacklist (prohibited from release), and 12 for the graylist (requiring scenario-based release, e.g., window control limited to speeds below 80 km/h, special scenario modes restricted to parking only). Expert consensus established safety red lines and design specifications, including “prohibition of voice control for core driving functions,” “adoption of the “action + object” command format,” and “requirement for secondary confirmation for safety-related functions.” The weighted total score across the six dimensions showed high consistency with the functional list (whitelist ≥ 7 points, blacklist <4.0 points), validating the model’s effectiveness. This method ensures scientific rigor while reducing the adaptation cycle to 15 days. It provides a practical, lightweight framework for rapid iteration in mass-production voice interaction projects.

Silent speech interfaces (SSIs) decode articulatory activity without audible speech. Although accelerometer-based SSIs can capture facial and neck movements in compact wearable setups, accelerometer-specific sensor placement has not been systematically examined. This study evaluated all combinations of ten accelerometers across the lower face and neck in a 100 English word silent speech classification task with 20 participants. Subject-dependent classification was performed using a convolutional neural network followed by a bidirectional long short-term memory network. Accuracy improved as the number of sensors increased, reaching a plateau with five sensors. At this point, Sensors 1 and 7, positioned over the upper and lower labial regions, Sensors 4 and 8, located bilaterally along the buccal-mandibular region, and Sensor 5, placed over the left submental region beneath the chin, achieved the highest accuracy of 92.30 ± 4.64% and were selected as the efficient configuration. These five sensors consistently ranked among the most informative locations in standalone performance, perturbation-based explainability, and sensor ablation analyses, indicating that they contributed unique and influential articulatory information. Regional coverage comparisons showed that configurations spanning broader functional articulatory regions outperformed those with more restricted coverage. This placement strategy was further validated using an independent 100-word vocabulary, demonstrating that broad regional coverage remained advantageous despite slight changes in the optimal sensor identities. A practical three-sensor configuration based on this strategy achieved approximately 90% recognition accuracy while substantially reducing hardware complexity. Together, these results support regionally distributed sensor placement as a design strategy for capturing complementary articulatory information in compact accelerometer-based SSI systems.

documents.abstract: Generative AI design tools make natural-language prompts a starting point for design, placing new articulation demands on designers. Rather than treating prompts as the transmission of preexisting intent, we ask how design intent is formed through situated interaction with AI. Five expert UI/UX designers (11–20 years’ experience, M = 15.4) designed landing-page hero sections with a generative AI tool, recorded through think-aloud and retrospective interviews. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we treated lexical granularity (L1 vibe, L2 design-domain, L3 operational language) as a sensitizing lens. Rather than moving from vibe to code unidirectionally, designers showed lexical oscillation, including returns from operational specificity to ambiguity. Mismatches with AI outputs became occasions to reconsider what they meant, and engagement shifted from instruction to consultation. One non-oscillating trajectory—a negative case—suggested conceptual misalignment as a tentative boundary. We position AI as a non-neutral generative interlocutor and ambiguity as a resource for design judgment.

Cognitive workload, musculoskeletal exposure, fatigue, and limited recovery can jointly affect worker comfort and task performance. However, these factors are often assessed separately, limiting the evaluation of cumulative ergonomic risk over time. This study proposes an integrated ergonomic modeling framework that combines cognitive workload, physical exposure, fatigue accumulation, and recovery within a common assessment structure. Normalized state variables are used to calculate a composite ergonomic risk index, and a proposed multi objective optimization procedure provides a basis for examining alternative task schedules and recovery intervals. Illustrative scenarios compare low, moderate, and high combined demands under specified model assumptions. The proposed analytical design also specifies a procedure for future sensitivity analysis of workload intensity, exposure duration, recovery rate, and worker susceptibility. The illustrative values indicate that higher modeled cognitive workload, physical exposure, and fatigue correspond to greater composite risk under the specified weighting scheme. However, these values are hypothetical and do not represent observed worker data or verified simulation outputs. The framework provides a methodological basis for examining relationships between modeled ergonomic risk and task performance during work schedule planning. Further research should implement reproducible computational experiments, conduct sensitivity analyses, and validate model predictions against measured workload, physical exposure, fatigue, and performance data before practical application.
